title: Atholl Brose
subtitle: A Scottish drink-dessert of oats, cream, whisky, and honey
excerpt: Toasted oats steeped in water to make a liquid, then mixed with double cream, runny honey, and Scotch whisky. Atholl brose sits between a drink and a dessert and has been made in Scotland since the fifteenth century.
sourceNotes: F. Marian McNeill, The Scots Kitchen (1929), Atholl brose as a traditional Scottish preparation with documented history from 1475. The name refers to the Earl of Atholl, who is said to have used the mixture to capture the rebel Iain MacDonald, Earl of Ross, by filling a well with it. McNeill gives several historical and contemporary versions.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate. Stir before serving as the oats settle.

content.text: Atholl brose is a Scottish preparation of oats, cream, honey, and whisky that functions somewhere between a drink and a pudding. The oats are soaked in water to make a thick liquid, which is then mixed with lightly whipped cream, honey, and Scotch whisky. Served in glasses with a spoon, it is particularly associated with Hogmanay and Burns Night.

items.prepNote: medium oatmeal or rolled oats, toasted briefly in a dry pan
runny, Scottish heather honey if available

content.text: Toast {{rolled-oats}} of oats in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until fragrant and lightly golden. Tip into a bowl.

Pour {{water}} of cold water over the oats and stir. Leave for 5 minutes. Strain through a sieve, pressing the oats to extract as much liquid as possible. Discard the solids or save them for porridge.
Whip {{double-cream}} of double cream to soft peaks: it should hold its shape but still flow slightly.
Combine the oat liquid, {{honey}} of honey, and {{whisky}} of whisky in a large bowl. Fold in the whipped cream until just combined. Taste and adjust the honey or whisky.
Pour into glasses and chill for at least 30 minutes before serving. Serve with a teaspoon alongside.

rows.symptom: Mixture is too thin and watery
rows.cause: Cream not whipped enough, or oat liquid too dilute
rows.fix: Whip the cream to soft peaks before folding. If the oat liquid seems very thin, use slightly less water when soaking.

rows.cause: Strong peated malt used, or ratio off
rows.fix: Use a lighter, non-peated malt whisky. Adjust the balance by adding more honey.

rows.symptom: Oat liquid is cloudy and thick
rows.cause: Oats soaked too long or pressed very hard through the sieve
rows.fix: 5 minutes soaking is enough. Press firmly but do not force the starchy solids through; a cloudy liquid is fine, a starchy paste is not.

rows.symptom: Cream collapses after sitting in the fridge
rows.cause: Cream over-whipped before folding, or stored too long
rows.fix: Whip to soft peaks only. Serve within 4 hours. Stir gently before serving if it separates slightly.

content.text: Atholl brose has been made in Scotland since at least the fifteenth century, when it first appears in written records. The name refers to the district of Atholl in Perthshire and, according to tradition, to a medieval story involving the capture of a rebel earl. F. Marian McNeill, in The Scots Kitchen , gives several versions of the recipe and notes its particular association with Hogmanay celebrations. It is now made primarily for Burns Night suppers (25 January) and Hogmanay (31 December).
